label: Person
name: Albert Malbois
summary:
Albert Malbois (1895–1979) was a French Capuchin bishop who served as a missionary in Morocco during the decades of the French Protectorate and into Moroccan independence. Born in France and ordained as a Capuchin friar, he was appointed to episcopal office in Morocco, where the Catholic community consisted primarily of French colonial settlers and military personnel.

Malbois's mission in Morocco was characteristic of French colonial Catholicism: his primary pastoral responsibility was to French Catholics living and working in the protectorate, rather than to the Muslim Moroccan majority among whom proselytism was prohibited. The Capuchin presence in Morocco had deep historical roots going back to the seventeenth century, when the order had been given responsibility for pastoral care of Christian captives and communities in North Africa.

Moroccan independence in 1956 transformed the Catholic community dramatically: as French settlers departed, the diocese's numbers fell precipitously, and the Church's mission shifted from serving a colonial population to maintaining a small diplomatic and service presence. Malbois's career bridged the colonial and post-colonial eras in North African Catholicism, representing the extraordinary transition from a Church of settlers to a Church of witness.
